title: [Vantage Point] The Senate’s Villar problem
summary: Putting former DPWH secretary Mark Villar in charge of the oversight desk looks less like legislative stewardship and more like institutional conflict of interest

blocks.text: Putting former DPWH secretary Mark Villar in charge of the oversight desk looks less like legislative stewardship and more like institutional conflict of interest

items: Senator Mark Villar's transition from the minority to the majority in the Senate raises concerns about institutional independence amid ongoing scrutiny of his family's business dealings and flood-control scandals.

Villar's appointment as chair of the Senate committee on public works, overseeing projects linked to his previous role as secretary of the Department of Public Works and Highways, presents a potential conflict of interest.

The timing of Villar's political maneuvering coincides with legal investigations into his family's business practices, prompting questions about the Senate's commitment to credible oversight and accountability.

As flood-control scandals raise uncomfortable questions about billions in infrastructure spending and his family’s corporate empire faces regulatory and legal scrutiny, Senator Mark Villar’s sudden leap to the majority—and into the public works committee chairmanship—puts a big question mark on the Senate’s institutional independence.
There are moments when the Senate seems bent on discovering just how far it can stretch the public’s capacity for disbelief.

While the floor was consumed by Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment proceedings, Senator Mark Villar executed a quiet migration from the minority to the majority. He did not arrive empty-handed. Without a peep of floor resistance, he walked away with two key levers of institutional influence: a seat on the Commission on Appointments and the chairmanship of the Senate committee on public works.

Meanwhile, across the aisle, his sister Camille stayed behind in the minority. It is the classic maneuver Filipinos know by instinct—namamangka sa dalawang ilog (playing both sides). Navigating both rivers at once guarantees that whatever current sweeps the chamber, the Villar family remains anchored on both banks.

blocks.caption: Mark Villar joins Senate majority | The wRap

blocks.text: They alone can speak to whether the split was coordinated, but in the transactional arithmetic of Philippine politics, having a foot in every camp is a survival strategy for any dynasty facing institutional heat. (READ: SEC chief Francis Lim to Villars: No family is too powerful to sue)
What makes this trade-off impossible to ignore is what Villar was handed: the legislative gavel over the very department he ran. (READ: DPWH post: Can Mark Villar rise above business interests?)

From 2016 to 2021, Mark Villar served as secretary of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) under Rodrigo Duterte. Those years sit squarely inside the timeline under review in the flood-control scandal, where billions of pesos in public funds yielded little more than submerged communities and unbuilt defenses. (READ: What’s a flood control project, anyway?)

When he was summoned to answer for projects greenlit under his watch, Villar denied improperly favoring family-linked contractors. Facing questions is not a finding of guilt. But it strains credibility to ask the public to trust that a Senate committee chair will fearlessly investigate his own administrative legacy. (READ: Firm owned by Senator Mark Villar’s uncle bagged P390M in flood control projects)
A committee chairmanship is not decorative. It sets the agenda, marshals witnesses, decides which scandals get dragged into daylight, and determines which files gather dust in an archive.

Even if Villar cannot award contracts from the rostrum, he holds the power to shape the inquiry. At an hour when taxpayers are demanding cold accounting for catastrophic flood projects, putting the former secretary in charge of the oversight desk looks less like legislative stewardship and more like institutional conflict of interest.

The legal entanglements do not end at the DPWH. Just this past September, the Ombudsman opened preliminary investigations into graft and administrative complaints against Villar family members, local water officials, and executives of PrimeWater over joint-venture agreements alleged to be disadvantageous to the public. Both Mark and Camille were named.

The family denies wrongdoing and insists it will defend itself through legal channels, but the fact remains: those agreements intersect directly with the years Mark sat in the Cabinet and held a seat on the Local Water Utilities Administration board.

Then came the afternoon’s corporate timing. Within an hour on Thursday, October 8, three Villar-controlled flagships—Vista Land & Lifescapes, Vistamalls, and VistaREIT—abruptly filed notices that their boards had cleared their long-overdue 2025 audited financial statements.

blocks.caption: Mark Villar switches camps. Minutes later, family’s troubled firms make their move.

blocks.text: These filings come after severe reporting delays led to trading suspensions across six Villar-linked firms. Board approval is not the same as audited accounts hitting the public tape, nor does it resolve overdue quarterly obligations.

Timing alone does not constitute evidence of backroom coordination, yet the optics are jarring: at the precise moment political power consolidated in the Senate, the family’s embattled business empire fired off a signal of operational survival.

This saga started in May 2025 when Vantage Point exposed the staggering arithmetic behind Villar Land—a P1.33-trillion property revaluation and an asserted profit of nearly a trillion pesos that quickly evaporated.

The subsequent reversal revealed the chasm between paper accounting and hard reality. Regulators soon disciplined the appraisal firm and launched complaints citing misleading disclosures, alleged market manipulation, and insider trading. The family denies wrongdoing, and due process must run its course, while AllDay and AllHome shutter retail outlets and Vista Land races to refinance debt.

This underscores the danger of letting private commercial distress collide with legislative oversight. Did Senate leaders ask a single hard question before handing him the committee? Did they demand recusal commitments for projects tied to his tenure or family enterprises? Who monitors the overseer?

Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri dismissed concerns by stating Villar’s party shift was unrelated to the impeachment fights. That may answer one concern, but it does nothing to clear the fog surrounding the public works gavel. When essential committees are handed out as political accommodations, legislative credibility disappears.

Filipinos have already paid the bill for suspect infrastructure, delayed dikes, and broken water projects. They should not also have to wonder if the Senate is running oversight with an eye toward preserving alliances. Like any citizen, Mark Villar is entitled to due process. But due process does not guarantee anyone the right to police their own past. The question is not whether he has the freedom to sit with the majority; he does. The real question is why the Senate decided to sacrifice the integrity of its own oversight just to give him a seat at the head of the table. – Rappler.com
